worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=3.33\,\text{min},$ we have

$$
3.33=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3.33}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=160\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=160{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=20\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
20=160{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33}\,\,
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}20 & =160{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33} \\ \frac{20}{160} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/3.33}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3.33} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3.33} \\ t & =\frac{3.33\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $10\,\text{min}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $20\,\mu \text{g}.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=20\,\mu \text{g}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{20\,\mu \text{g}}{160\,\mu \text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $3$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $160\,\mu \text{g}$ to $20\,\mu \text{g}.$ Hence,

$$
t=3\cdot {t}_{1/2}=3\cdot 3.33\,\text{min}≈10\,\text{min}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $10\,\text{min}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $20\,\mu \text{g}.$

M′(t)=−kM(t),M(0)=M0.

The general solution to this equation is

M(t)=M0e−kt.

The half-life t1/2 is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

t1/2=ln⁡2k.

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

Method 1

Since we know that t1/2=3.33min, we have

3.33=ln⁡2k⇒k=ln⁡23.33

Also, since M0=160μg, we have the particular solution

M(t)=160e−tln⁡2/3.33.

We wish to calculate the time t such that M(t)=20μg. So, we set up our equation as follows:

20=160e−tln⁡2/3.33

Solving this equation for t, we get

20=160e−tln⁡2/3.3320160=e−tln⁡2/3.3318=e−tln⁡2/3.33ln⁡(18)=ln⁡(e−tln⁡2/3.33)ln⁡1−ln⁡8=−tln⁡23.33−ln⁡8=−tln⁡23.33t=3.33⋅ln⁡8ln⁡2t≈10.

Therefore, we conclude that it takes 10min for the mass of the substance to reduce to 20μg.

Method 2

We wish to calculate the time t such that M(t)=20μg. Notice that

M(t)M(0)=20μg160μg=18=(12)3,

or equivalently

M(t)=(12)3⋅M(0).

From this equation, we see that 3 half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from 160μg to 20μg. Hence,

t=3⋅t1/2=3⋅3.33min≈10min.

Therefore, we conclude that it takes 10min for the mass of the substance to reduce to 20μg.
